body: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports serverless model customization for Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8 27B, and Ministral 3 3B, 8B, and 14B models. In addition to deploying these models on SageMaker AI, you can now adapt them to your specific domains and workflows, using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) techniques. You can also adapt these models with either low-rank adaptation (LoRA) or full fine-tuning techniques. This launch adds these models to a wide variety of models available for serverless customization on SageMaker AI, including models from the Nova, Gemma 4, Nemotron 3.5, Qwen, Llama, gpt-oss, and DeepSeek families. Model customization lets you tailor foundation models with your proprietary data so a smaller, right-sized model can match frontier-model quality on your tasks, while also reducing cost and latency. You can use labeled data with SFT to improve accuracy on domain-specific tasks, preference data with DPO to align outputs with your organization's tone, or reward signals with RFT to improve performance on new tasks. With serverless customization, SageMaker AI handles all infrastructure provisioning and training orchestration, so you can focus on your data and evaluation rather than cluster management, and only pay for what you use. Serverless model customization on SageMaker AI is available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To get started, navigate to the Models page in Amazon SageMaker Studio to launch a customization job, use the SageMaker Python SDK or use our Agent skills with your choice of coding assistant. To learn more and see the full supported list of models, see the Amazon SageMaker AI model customization documentation .

title: Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports partial indexes
body: Amazon Aurora DSQL now lets you build an index over a specific subset of a table, storing only qualifying rows rather than every row in the entire table, which improves query performance and lowers index storage cost. Many tables hold a small working set alongside a much larger history, such as open orders among years of completed ones. Add a WHERE clause to CREATE INDEX to index just that working set. The index stays small as the table grows, and queries that target those rows read less data. Aurora DSQL uses a partial index for any query whose filter falls within the index's condition. Partial indexes are available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available. To learn more, see CREATE INDEX in the Aurora DSQL User Guide.

title: AWS Agent Registry now supports custom metadata for registry records
body: AWS Agent Registry is the centralized, governed catalog for agents, MCP servers, agent skills, gateways, and custom resources within your organization. As organizations scale to hundreds of such resources, a name and description alone are insufficient for effective governance and discovery. Custom metadata lets you extend every registry record with your organization's own structured fields, so both people and automated systems can find and govern resources consistently. With custom metadata, publishers can record fields like team ownership, data classification, or review status directly on each registry record. You define a schema once per registry with common attributes, then extend it with type-specific fields — such as a model family for agent records. Each field supports free text, a URL, a Boolean, or a choice from a list of allowed values, and the registry validates required fields and values on every record creation or update. You can then filter search results on any custom metadata field from the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, or the registry's MCP endpoint. Custom metadata is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To learn more, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation . For detailed setup guidance, see Define a custom metadata schema and Set custom metadata values on a record .

title: AWS announces AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Megaport
body: AWS launches AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Megaport, a fully managed connectivity offering that allows customers to connect their branch offices, data centers, and remote locations to AWS with just a few clicks, eliminating the friction and complexity of network setup. As a milestone collaboration between AWS and Megaport, AWS Interconnect - last mile combines AWS cloud innovation with Megaport operating one of the world's largest Software Defined Networks (SDN), with 1,200+ enabled data centers across 31 countries. Through the AWS Management Console, customers can now instantly establish private, high-speed connections to AWS by simply choosing their preferred AWS Region, bandwidth speed, Direct Connect Gateway ID and partner subscriber ID. Once initiated, AWS generates an activation key to complete connectivity provisioning with Megaport. The launch simplifies the connectivity experience by pre-provisioning capacity and automating complex network configuration including BGP peering, VLAN configuration, and ASN assignment. At GA, customers will also be able to dynamically scale bandwidth from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps through the AWS Console. The service is designed for high availability, with zero down-time maintenance, backed by a 99.99% SLA. AWS Interconnect - last mile is available in the San Jose (us-west-1) and N. Virginia (us-east-1) metros through Megaport. You can create a preview Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, Command Line Interface (CLI), or API. Partners can also easily adopt via a published open API package on GitHub . For more information, see the AWS Interconnect - last mile documentation and pricing pages .

title: AWS Batch now publishes job metrics to Amazon CloudWatch
body: AWS Batch now publishes job metrics to Amazon CloudWatch, providing native observability for batch workloads. AWS Batch emits metrics throughout the job lifecycle, giving you visibility into job queue health, failure rates, and job durations. AWS Batch automatically publishes job state transition and duration metrics to the AWS/Batch namespace in Amazon CloudWatch, with JobQueueName dimension. State transition metrics track how many jobs entered a given state, such as submitted, running, succeeded, or failed. Duration metrics track how long jobs spent between states, such as time from submission to runnable or total execution time. You can view these metrics in the AWS Batch console, the Amazon CloudWatch console, or through the AWS CLI and AWS SDKs. AWS Batch CloudWatch metrics are now published in all AWS Regions where AWS Batch is available. For more information, see CloudWatch Metrics page in the AWS Batch User Guide .

title: AWS Clean Rooms now supports Databricks as a data source
body: AWS Clean Rooms now supports Databricks as a data source , so collaboration members and their partners can securely analyze data managed in Databricks without moving or revealing the source data. Members query a Databricks table shared through Delta Sharing directly in a collaboration. Databricks joins AWS Glue, Snowflake, and Amazon Athena as supported data sources in AWS Clean Rooms. Previously, members with data in Databricks had to export or replicate it into Amazon S3 to use it as a table in a collaboration, which added pipeline work and an extra copy of the data to govern. Now members can register a Databricks table directly by providing the workspace URL, schema, and table along with a Delta Sharing share, and make it available to a collaboration. For example, a retailer that manages its customer data in Databricks can collaborate with a media partner on campaign measurement in AWS Clean Rooms, running approved analyses against its Databricks data without first building and maintaining an export to S3. AWS Clean Rooms helps companies and their partners easily analyze and collaborate on their collective datasets without revealing or copying one another’s underlying data. For more information about the AWS Regions where AWS Clean Rooms is available, see the AWS Regions table. To learn more about collaborating with AWS Clean Rooms, visit AWS Clean Rooms .

title: AWS End User Messaging now offers managed OTP verification end-to-end
body: Today, AWS End User Messaging announces end-to-end managed one-time passcode (OTP) verification in Notify. You get a working OTP solution in under five minutes, including AWS phone numbers and code verification, without setting up a phone number, registering with carriers, or managing how messages are delivered. Before, you generated the passcode yourself and passed it to Notify to send, and you built and maintained the logic to create, store, and expire codes. Now Notify generates the code, delivers it, and verifies the code the recipient enters, so you ship a complete verification flow and skip that work entirely. You can deliver codes over text, voice, and now WhatsApp. You set the rules once in a notify code configuration: the code type, length, how long it stays valid, and how many attempts a recipient gets, along with your templates for each channel. From then on, one call sends a code to a recipient on the channel you choose, and another checks the code they enter. Notify is available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS End User Messaging is available. To learn more and get started, see the AWS End User Messaging User Guide.

title: AWS End User Messaging now supports Brand Profiles
body: Today, AWS End User Messaging announces Brand Profiles, which let you store your brand and company information once and reuse it across your messaging registrations. To send messages on SMS, RCS, and WhatsApp, you register your brand with carriers and messaging providers, and today you fill in the same company details, address, contact information, and use case by hand on every form, for each channel and country. That repeated entry slows every new registration, and a typo or other error can get one rejected and delay when you can start sending. With Brand Profiles, you enter this information once and apply it to each new registration, so you register faster and keep your details consistent across channels and countries. You can use Brand Profiles whether you send for your own brand or manage several brands in a single AWS account. When you start a registration with a Brand Profile, the service fills in the matching fields from the information you saved and gives you a draft to review before you submit. By default, it matches standard fields such as company name, tax ID, address, and contact details. You can also turn on smart match, which uses AI to fill in fields even when their names differ. You can build a Brand Profile from scratch or start from your existing registrations. Brand Profiles is available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS End User Messaging is available. To learn more and get started, see the AWS End User Messaging User Guide.

title: AWS HealthOmics expands container registry support for private workflows
body: You can now use container images from registries such as Seqera (Wave), NVIDIA NGC, and Google Artifact Registry with AWS HealthOmics expanded support for third-party container registries. You can use the containerized tools your workflows already rely on, without manually migrating images into Amazon ECR or editing your workflow definitions. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. With expanded container registry support, you can now instruct HealthOmics to copy container images, on your behalf, from newly supported registries into your Amazon ECR when running your private workflows. Previously, AWS HealthOmics could pull images only from registries supported through Amazon ECR pull-through cache (PTC). Your private workflows can now access Amazon ECR pull-through cache registries and the newly supported third party container registries, so you do not need to pull, re-push, or rewrite image URIs yourself. Expanded container registry support is now available in all AWS Regions where HealthOmics is available: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Singapore, Seoul, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the third-party container image support documentation .

title: AWS IAM Identity Center's Identity Store now supports change notifications through Amazon EventBridge
body: AWS IAM Identity Center's Identity Store now delivers real-time events to Amazon EventBridge when users, groups, or group memberships or the identity store itself is created, updated, or deleted. AWS IAM Identity Center Identity Store is a central repository that allows you to manage identities and access across AWS accounts and applications, serving as the identity source for AWS IAM Identity Center. This new capability helps you automatically respond to identity lifecycle events and support your security and compliance processes by detecting changes as they happen. With Identity Store change notifications, you can build automated workflows that respond to identity changes in your organization. For example, security teams can create EventBridge rules that trigger AWS Lambda functions to audit user provisioning activity, send alerts to security information and event management (SIEM) systems, or update access in downstream applications when users or groups change. Organizations that manage large workforces can also use this data to automate onboarding and offboarding when users are added to or removed from specific groups. Change notifications are available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available, and events are sent in each enabled Region of your instance. For the list of Regions, see AWS capabilities by Regions . Change notifications are available at no additional cost beyond standard Amazon EventBridge usage charges. To learn more, see Event notifications in the AWS IAM Identity Center User Guide and Identity Store events in the Amazon EventBridge Events Reference.

title: AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances
body: AWS Lambda now supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) for lazy loading Event Functions packaged as Open Container Initiative (OCI) images running on Lambda Managed Instances . With SOCI support, Lambda fetches only the files needed at each stage of the execution environment startup rather than downloading the entire image upfront, reducing container startup times by up to 70%. Customers building compute-intensive applications such as data processing pipelines, high-throughput API backends, and batch computation workloads require substantial memory and CPU resources to process large datasets, serve low-latency responses at scale, and run complex computations efficiently. Container images for these workloads can reach several gigabytes, and downloading and preparing the full image can take several minutes when provisioning new execution environments. SOCI support on Lambda Managed Instances eliminates this bottleneck by streaming only the required files at each stage of the execution environment startup, so your functions start faster as you scale. To get started, create a SOCI index (a table of contents for the files in your image layers) for your container image and push it to Amazon ECR . When creating or updating your function, set the image URI to the SOCI-indexed tag in Amazon ECR (for example, my-function:v1-soci) and publish a function version. Lambda automatically detects the SOCI index and enables lazy loading with no additional configuration. If you use a coding assistant such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex, install the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS to configure and deploy functions through your agent. The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Managed Instances developer guide .

title: AWS Network Firewall adds wildcard support for container attribute filters
body: AWS Network Firewall now supports wildcard matching in container attribute-based inspection filters for Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). This enhancement allows you to define attribute filters using wildcard patterns to match multiple container workloads in a single rule, eliminating the need to create individual container associations for each variant. With wildcard support, you can use patterns like app=payments-* to automatically cover all variants of an application, such as payments-api, payments-worker, and payments-cron. This simplifies firewall rule management for dynamic container environments where new application variants are frequently deployed, reducing operational overhead and ensuring consistent security coverage across your containerized workloads. Wildcard support for container attribute filters is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Network Firewall container attribute-based inspection is supported. For a full list of supported Regions, see the AWS Region Table . To get started, visit AWS Network Firewall product page and service documentation .

title: AWS Security Hub introduces remediation plans to prioritize and fix security exposures
body: AWS Security Hub now offers remediation plans that group related exposure findings sharing a root cause. Instead of addressing each exposure individually, you can now fix a single underlying resource, such as a misconfigured setting or overly permissive policy, and resolve or reduce the severity of multiple exposures at once. Each remediation plan includes prioritization guidance (Critical, High, Medium, or Low), impact assessment, and detailed step-by-step instructions with examples in multiple formats including AWS CLI, Terraform, CloudFormation, Python, and CDK. Security Hub automatically prioritizes plans so those reducing the most risk appear first, helping you focus remediation efforts where they matter most. AI agents can also programmatically consume remediation plans through the API to automate security fixes across your environment. Remediation plans are available in every AWS Region where AWS Security Hub is available and at no additional cost under AWS Security Hub Essentials plan. To learn more, visit the AWS Security Hub documentation .

title: AWS Transform now builds new networks and modernizes security groups
body: AWS Transform for migrations now gives you three ways to bring your network to AWS. In addition to migrating and modernizing your existing network, you can build a new network from scratch or convert your on-premises access rules into optimized security groups and deploy them into existing VPCs. Whichever path you choose, you arrive on AWS with a secure and scalable network foundation. On-premises networks accumulate years of definitions and access rules that you may not want to carry to AWS as-is. For a clean start, AWS Transform builds a new network aligned to AWS best practices. To bring your access rules with you, AWS Transform converts them into security groups and modernizes them as it goes, detecting stale rules and recommending optimizations, then deploys the groups into your existing VPCs without redeploying your network stack. These capabilities allow you migrate to any AWS commercial or GovCloud Region . To get started, see Migrate networks . To learn more, visit AWS Transform for migrations .

title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now supports Standard tier for contextual grounding checks
body: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now offers a Standard tier for contextual grounding checks, which detect and filter hallucinations by checking whether a model response is grounded in your reference source and relevant to the user's query. The Standard tier is more robust than the Classic tier. It supports responses that include reasoning or conversational content, scores differently worded responses with the same meaning more consistently, and provides more comprehensive language support, matching the Standard tier for content filters and denied topics. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safeguards for generative AI applications on any foundation model through the ApplyGuardrail API. Until now, contextual grounding checks applied strict grounding suited to summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. With the Standard tier, you can also apply contextual grounding checks to conversational applications and to responses that reason over the source. You choose the tier for each guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock console or API. Existing guardrails keep the Classic tier until you change them. Pricing is the same for both tiers. To use the Standard tier, your guardrail must use cross-Region inference with a guardrail profile. The Standard tier for contextual grounding checks is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Milan), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation on contextual grounding checks and safeguard tiers , or visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails product page .

title: Announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS for node bootstrapping
body: For blockchain node operators running Ethereum or Solana, AWS is announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS, an initiative that publishes pre-synced public blockchain node chain data in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) so you can bootstrap a node from a snapshot instead of peer-to-peer syncing from the network. These snapshots are hosted on Amazon S3 within AWS infrastructure, enabling customers running nodes on AWS benefit from reduced latency and optimized data transfer. Blockchain Snapshots on AWS republishes each network's authoritative snapshot in a format optimized for parallel extraction across multiple cores, reducing setup time, that an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance can use. Snapshots cover Ethereum and Solana, are available at no charge, and refresh on the same cadence as the upstream provider. Use them to add capacity to a remote procedure call (RPC) fleet, recover a failed node, or re-sync a corrupted database. You can use Blockchain Snapshots on AWS in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Ireland), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). Access requires an Amazon EC2 instance in the same Region with an Amazon S3 gateway VPC endpoint. To get started, visit the Blockchain Snapshots on AWS documentation to access setup instructions and download the latest snapshots.

title: Claude Haiku 5.5 is now available on AWS
body: AWS now offers Claude Haiku 5.5, the fastest and most efficient model in the Claude 5.5 family, built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it costs around 75% less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. Claude Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic's most capable Haiku yet, a significant step up from Haiku 4.5 across coding, tool use, computer use, and agents. It's also the first Haiku with effort controls, so teams can tune cost against intelligence for each task. Haiku 5.5 fits work where speed and cost matter most: real-time experiences like voice agents, live support, and in-app assistants, and high-volume tasks like classification, summarization, and pulling key fields from documents. It's also a fast, cost-efficient subagent. A more capable model like Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand off well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku, making it practical to run many agents in parallel. Customers have two ways to access Claude Haiku 5.5: Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Amazon Bedrock gives you Haiku's capabilities while keeping your data within AWS infrastructure with regional data residency and provides access through a unified service with AWS-managed features like Guardrails and Knowledge Bases. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation and regional availability . Claude Platform on AWS gives you direct access to Anthropic's native platform experience and capabilities via the AWS Console. Build, test, and deploy with the same APIs, features, and console experience you'd get working with Anthropic directly, unified with AWS billing and authentication. To get started, see the Claude Platform on AWS documentation.

title: Amazon CloudFront now supports AWS Lambda Web Functions as an origin
body: Starting today, you can deliver web applications built on AWS Lambda Web Functions through CloudFront's global edge network. With CloudFront in front of a Lambda Web Function, you get TLS termination at the edge for lower latency and faster connections, caching for better performance, and custom domains with managed TLS certificates. No changes to application code are needed. CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) restricts your Lambda Web Function so it's reachable only through CloudFront, so unintended requests that bypass your security protections do not reach your origin. With OAC in place, CloudFront's edge network protects your Lambda Web Function from network-layer DDoS attacks, and you can attach AWS WAF for additional application-layer security. For applications that authenticate their own users, OAC ensures that original credentials reach the application unchanged, so existing sign-in flows keep working. CloudFront support for AWS Lambda Web Functions is available worldwide, except in the CloudFront China region. To get started, use the CloudFront Console, SDK, CLI, or CloudFormation to configure your Lambda Web Function as a CloudFront origin. For more information, refer to the CloudFront Developer Guide . There are no additional fees associated with this feature.

title: Amazon Connect Customer supports inline attachment previews
body: Amazon Connect Customer lets agents preview attachments directly in the agent workspace, reducing contact handling time and limiting the need to download sensitive customer information. Agents can preview PDFs, images, and text files across email, chat, and cases, navigate between attachments, and view multi-page documents without leaving the conversation. Amazon Connect Customer attachment previews is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London) regions . To learn more and get started, please refer to the help documentation or visit the Amazon Connect Customer website.

title: Amazon Connect Customer launches two new layouts for agent workspace
body: Amazon Connect Customer now offers two different layouts that optimize screen space on the agent workspace. Contact center agents spend hours each day in the agent workspace, which includes all of the contact controls and applications they need to resolve customer issues. Agents who handle different channels and workflows want the workspace arranged differently, so that they can quickly read, respond, and access their tools. Now, administrators can choose the best layout for each team, maximizing agent efficiency and satisfaction. On the Modern layout, contact controls are at the top of the workspace, maximizing screen space for the applications beneath during voice calls. When agents handle chat, email, and task contacts on the Modern layout, they now have a taller, wider area to read and respond. The Classic layout offers a familiar experience for agents already using the agent workspace, now with contact controls that expand and contract by channel and a resizable agent assist application. Administrators can assign the Modern layout to a team migrating from another agent desktop with controls at the top, while teams already familiar with the agent workspace can use the Classic layout. You can use the new layouts for the Amazon Connect Customer agent workspace in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). To learn more and get started, see the agent workspace in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

title: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports FSx for OpenZFS, NFS 4.2, and object metadata controls
body: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports Amazon FSx for OpenZFS as a source or destination location, NFS version 4.2 for on-premises NFS servers and FSx for OpenZFS file systems, and a new ObjectMetadata option for object storage transfers. Previously, customers transferring data to or from FSx for OpenZFS were limited to Basic mode. NFS 4.2 lets you transfer data from NFS servers on the latest version without reconfiguring them to an older protocol version. The ObjectMetadata option gives you control over whether an object's user metadata is copied to the destination, which helps when destination metadata must stay intact, such as buckets served by AWS Storage Gateway, or when source metadata keys are not compatible with the destination, such as Azure Blob Storage. Existing tasks remain unaffected and continue to run as scheduled. These capabilities are available for Enhanced mode tasks in all AWS Regions where AWS DataSync Enhanced mode is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS DataSync documentation .

title: Amazon EC2 introduces shared tags for Amazon Machine Images
body: Amazon EC2 now supports AMI tag sharing, a new feature that lets AMI owners make selected tags visible to all AWS accounts an AMI is shared with. Whether an AMI is shared with an account, across an organization, or made public, a shared tag is automatically shared alongside the AMI, eliminating the need to build and maintain custom tag replication workflows. AMI owners simply add the 'ec2:SharedTag/' prefix to any tag key, and every account the AMI is shared with can immediately see it. This removes the operational burden of replicating tags into each account after sharing an AMI. Shared tags are read-only for recipient accounts, so only the owner can create, modify, or delete them. They count only against the owner's 50 tag per resource quota, allowing recipient accounts to continue adding their own private tags without any impact to their limits. This feature is available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost. To learn more, please visit the documentation and read the blog .

title: Amazon ECS Managed Instances adds cross-instance and Spot consolidation
body: Today, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Managed Instances introduces two infrastructure optimization updates: cross-instance and Spot consolidation. Cross-instance consolidation evaluates tasks running across multiple underutilized instances together, packing them onto fewer instances to raise utilization and lower costs. Spot consolidation extends this capability to Spot capacity, consolidating underutilized Spot Instances after first verifying replacement capacity is available. Amazon ECS Managed Instances provisions, configures, and operates right-sized Amazon EC2 instances for your workloads, balancing availability and cost. Its infrastructure optimization continuously monitors your fleet, reclaiming idle capacity and consolidating underutilized instances with graceful start-before-stop task replacement. Until now, optimization evaluated each instance in isolation for replacement, which worked well when a capacity provider was configured with diverse instance types. However, when a capacity provider was configured with a narrow range of instance types, there were fewer opportunities to consolidate multiple underutilized instances, because no single replacement could yield savings. With cross-instance consolidation, ECS now evaluates and repacks tasks across multiple instances simultaneously. For example, in our testing with a capacity provider configured for c9g instances with a minimum size of 4xlarge, running 261 tasks (each 1 vCPU, 1.94 GiB), cross-instance consolidation reduced the fleet from 19 instances (seven 4xlarge, seven 8xlarge, four 12xlarge, and one 24xlarge) to 13 instances (eight 4xlarge and five 8xlarge), while raising CPU utilization from 42% to 91% and memory utilization from 41% to 88%. Spot consolidation applies the same approach to Spot capacity, first verifying replacement capacity is available. With these enhancements, ECS Managed Instances delivers deeper cost optimization for both your On-Demand and Spot workloads. Cross-instance and Spot consolidation are now available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions, and apply automatically to all existing and new ECS Managed Instances capacity providers. To learn more, see our documentation .

title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now supports changing durability on existing clusters
body: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now lets you enable or disable durability on your existing node-based clusters. Previously, you couldn't change the durability configuration of an existing cluster in place. This made it harder to move from caching to persistent data store use cases, or to adapt as your application requirements change. Now you can change durability at any point in your application's lifecycle. You can choose between two durability options: synchronous and asynchronous writes. Synchronous writes persist data across at least two AZs before responding to the client, designed for zero data loss at single-digit millisecond write latency. Asynchronous writes persist data after responding to the client, maintaining microsecond write latency at no additional cost. However, up to 10 seconds of uncommitted data could be lost in the rare event of a failure. Both options maintain microsecond read latency. You can now use ElastiCache for a broader set of use cases beyond caching where data loss is unacceptable such as AI agent long-term memory, AI agent workflow state, knowledge bases for RAG applications, payment tokenization, and real-time inventory management. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where ElastiCache for Valkey 9.0 and later is available. To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS SDK, or AWS CLI. For pricing, see the Amazon ElastiCache pricing page . To learn more, see Durability in the ElastiCache documentation.

title: Amazon GuardDuty now supports centralized management using AWS Organizations declarative policies
body: Amazon GuardDuty now supports AWS Organizations declarative policies, enabling you to centrally enable GuardDuty threat detection across every account and Region in your AWS organization. Using an organization policy, you can now apply a centrally managed GuardDuty enablement configuration. The configuration applies to existing accounts and is automatically maintained as new accounts join your organization. Enabling GuardDuty across all relevant accounts and Regions helps ensure comprehensive threat detection coverage. Previously, keeping enablement aligned across a large multi-account, multi-Region environment meant configuring GuardDuty's enablement settings separately in each Region, which could drift over time. Now you can define a central GuardDuty policy from your delegated administrator account that sets an enablement baseline across your organization (at the organization root, OUs, or individual accounts). The policy supports a default configuration that applies in every Region where GuardDuty is available, as well as per-Region overrides for Regions that require different enablement. Enablement set by a policy cannot be overridden via the GuardDuty console or API. GuardDuty declarative policy support is available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, make sure the delegated administrator has permission to manage GuardDuty policies. Then, sign in to the GuardDuty console and choose Organization policies, or create a policy programmatically using AWS Organizations APIs. To learn more, see Managing accounts using organization policies in the Amazon GuardDuty User Guide and Amazon GuardDuty policies in the AWS Organizations User Guide.

title: AWS IAM Identity Center simplifies identity source changes from Active Directory
body: AWS IAM Identity Center now retains your workforce identities and their assignments when you change your identity source from Active Directory to an external identity provider (IdP), such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, or to the Identity Center directory. Specifically, it preserves your users, groups, group memberships, permission set assignments, and application assignments. Previously, this change required you to recreate them in IAM Identity Center. IAM Identity Center helps you connect your workforce identities to AWS once and manage their access centrally across AWS applications and accounts. When you change your identity source from Active Directory, your existing identity store remains in place, so your users and groups keep the same IDs. As a result, users retain their access to AWS accounts and applications, and policies that reference your user IDs, group IDs, or identity store ID continue to work. To make this change, configure your new identity source with the standard setup required for users to sign in. After the change, your workforce signs in through your dual-stack AWS access portal URL. Changing your identity source in the other direction, to Active Directory, works as before. This feature is available for organization instances of IAM Identity Center in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available. IAM Identity Center is provided at no additional cost. To get started, navigate to the IAM Identity Center console. For more information, see Change your identity source in the IAM Identity Center User Guide. To learn more about IAM Identity Center, visit the product detail page .

title: Amazon Lightsail CDN distributions now support web application firewall
body: Amazon Lightsail CDN distributions now support integrated Web Application Firewall (WAF) capabilities, giving customers a simple, built-in way to protect their web applications. Previously, Lightsail distributions lacked native web application firewall capabilities, leaving customers without an easy-to-configure layer of protection. Lightsail now offers distribution plans with WAF capability at no additional cost. Lightsail's distribution plans can block common web exploits, malicious request patterns, traffic from anonymizing services (e.g. VPNs, proxies, and Tor nodes), SQL injection, OS-level attacks, PHP application-layer vulnerabilities, automated bot activity, and account takeover attempts. Once enabled, customers can monitor allowed and blocked requests through distribution metrics to maintain visibility into their site traffic. On the Lightsail console , you can enable WAF on the Security tab when you manage your distribution and monitor filtered requests on the Metrics tab. You can also enable WAF using the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI) or AWS SDKs. To learn more about enabling WAF for your Lightsail distributions, visit the Amazon Lightsail documentation .

title: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports high bitrate mode
body: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports high bitrate modes with two new tiers: 250 Mbps and 500 Mbps. This allows professional broadcasters that need higher bitrates to transport high-value content without compromising quality or reliability. This enhancement enables industry-standard workflows such as VSF TR-07 compliant transport stream distribution for broadcast contribution, content distribution, and remote production. High bitrate mode supports up to two redundant sources for reliability and includes data plane optimizations that reduce jitter for improved performance. To learn more, visit the AWS Elemental MediaConnect product page and the MediaConnect pricing page .

title: AWS Network Firewall now supports Route 53 Resolved IP Validation
body: AWS Network Firewall now supports IP validation, extending domain-based filtering beyond HTTP/HTTPS to protocols such as SFTP and SSH. This new capability validates that a connection's destination IP address was resolved through your VPC's Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver, closing security gaps where clients could bypass domain rules. This feature enables Network Firewall customers to implement domain filtering rules for any protocol, not just HTTP/HTTPS, providing more flexible security policies than IP-based rules alone. It simplifies protection against Server Name Identifier (SNI) spoofing by validating the IPs resolved by the Route 53 VPC Resolver against the SNI, ensuring traffic only reaches legitimately resolved destinations. Organizations can now enforce consistent domain-based security policies across all outbound traffic types, from web applications to file transfer protocols, without complex workarounds. Additionally, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall can be used with your VPC Resolver for extended DNS security. Resolved IP validation is available in all AWS commercial regions where AWS Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available, at no additional charge. For a full list of supported regions, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page . To learn more, visit AWS Network Firewall product page and service documentation .

title: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports index-level encryption
body: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports index-level encryption, letting you encrypt each index at rest with its own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. This helps you protect data with different ownership or sensitivity under separate keys on the same domain. For example, you can encrypt each tenant's data with its own key in a multi-tenant application. Index-level encryption builds on the existing encryption at rest capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service. To enable it, set the encryption mode to Native and specify a customer managed AWS KMS key when you create a new domain using the AWS Management Console or the AWS CLI. You can then register additional keys with the domain and use them to encrypt individual indexes. Index-level encryption is available for domains running OpenSearch version 3.3 or later in 14 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Paris), and South America (São Paulo). There is no additional charge for the feature. Standard AWS KMS and OpenSearch Service charges apply. To get started, see Index-level encryption in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

title: AWS Partner Central launches Program Navigator, Case Study Generator, and streamlined specialization review
body: AWS Partner Central now features Program Navigator, a unified experience that lets partners discover, apply for, and track AWS Specialization program applications in one place. Partners can browse specialization designations, view requirements and benefits, and submit applications through a guided, step-by-step workflow. The new Case Study Generator in AWS Partner Central gives partners a redesigned creation experience with three starting paths: build a case study directly with AI assistance, import from an existing customer success story URL, or auto-populate from an opportunity. Case studies created for go-to-market purposes now follow a streamlined review path, a lightweight policy validation that lets partners publish directly to AWS domains without a specialization review. The deeper specialization-level review applies only to case studies associated with Program Navigator applications. Additionally, AWS has streamlined the specialization application review process through Program Navigator. Partners submitting applications can expect faster review times and more detailed, requirement-level feedback throughout the process. Partners applying for non-specialization programs continue to access those programs through the existing experience. Program Navigator and Case Study Generator are available to all AWS Partners in AWS Partner Central . To get started, navigate to Program Navigator and Case Studies under the Go to Market section in the left navigation panel.

title: Quick now supports smart approvals for agentic actions
body: Amazon Quick now supports smart approvals, a review layer that reduces unnecessary approval prompts while preserving human oversight of the actions that matter most. As agents take more actions on a user's behalf, such as sending email, updating records, and creating tickets, asking a person to approve every step leads to approval fatigue and weaker oversight over time. With smart approvals, a separate review model called the classifier evaluates each eligible action against the user's request. It approves routine actions automatically and refers consequential actions to the user for review. Your existing policies always come first. Smart approvals only reviews actions where the user's setting is "ask" each time. Denied actions stay denied, and smart approvals never grants new access. The classifier sends higher-impact actions to the user for review. These include sending content outside the organization, changing permissions, deleting content, making payments, and actions that go beyond what the user asked for. Each automatic approval covers only the exact action that was reviewed. If a review fails or times out, the action goes to the user. Smart approvals is on for all users by default. Administrators control who can use it with custom permissions, and users can turn it off for their conversations and scheduled runs in chat options. AWS CloudTrail records each action review made through smart approvals and each change to a user's smart approvals setting. Smart approvals is available in Amazon Quick in all AWS Regions where Amazon Quick agentic capabilities are supported. For more information, see the AWS Region table . To learn more about smart approvals, see smart approvals in the Amazon Quick User Guide. For more information about Amazon Quick, see the Amazon Quick product page .

title: Amazon Redshift now supports cross-Region queries for your data lake
body: Amazon Redshift now supports querying Amazon S3 data lake tables located in a different AWS Region. With enhanced VPC routing, data lake query traffic between Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift stays within your own VPC. Both capabilities are powered by the integrated data lake query engine that runs directly on the compute of RG provisioned and Serverless clusters. These features are aimed at enterprises with globally distributed data and at security-sensitive customers who need tight control over how their data travels. With cross-Region support, you can use Amazon Redshift to query S3 data in another Region directly, without first copying or replicating it. This makes it easier to run global analytics, consolidate reporting across Regions, and query data that must remain in a specific Region for residency requirements. Cross-Region queries incur standard data transfer charges. Because the query engine runs on your cluster's compute, data moving between Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift flows entirely over your VPC when you use enhanced VPC routing, never over public networks. Regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare, and government benefit from this feature as it keeps data lake queries within the network boundaries their compliance requirements demand. Both capabilities work with the integrated data lake query engine, which is available in all regions where RG provisioned and Serverless clusters are available. To learn more, see Querying your data lake tables with enhanced VPC routing in the Amazon Redshift documentation .

title: Amazon ECR now supports replication backfill for existing container images
body: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports replication backfill, enabling you to replicate existing images in your private registry to your configured replication registry destinations. Previously, replication only applied to images pushed after the replication configuration was enabled, requiring customers to manually retag images to trigger replication of preexisting images. With replication backfill, you can now replicate your full image catalog to new or existing destinations with a single API call. Replication backfill is useful when expanding to a new AWS Region, validating disaster recovery readiness, updating replication rules, or ensuring complete image catalogs exist across Regions for compliance purposes. You can run up to ten backfill jobs concurrently, monitor progress and per-image results through new APIs, and stop a job at any time without deleting images that have already been replicated. Replication backfill is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is available. To learn more, refer to the Amazon ECR user guide .

title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports custom sequence lengths for serverless model customization jobs
body: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI announces the ability to configure the sequence length used during your serverless model customization job. Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization supports fine-tuning for many open-weight models, including models from popular families including gpt-oss, Gemma, Llama, Nemotron, and Qwen. Previously, each fine-tuning recipe ran at a fixed sequence length that customers could not modify. Customers sometimes need to modify these parameters to achieve better results for their use case. Customers also asked for longer sequence lengths than the static defaults we supported on some models. Now, you can set sequence length parameters as part of the customization job's hyperparameters, anywhere up to the published maximum for your chosen model and technique. You can set the dataset_max_len hyperparameter for SFT and DPO jobs or set max_prompt_length and max_response_length hyperparameters for RFT jobs. This gives you more control to match your training data characteristics, whether you are working with short question-answer pairs or multi-page documents. Published maximums are up to 16K tokens for many models depending on model and technique. Serverless model customization on SageMaker AI is available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To get started, navigate to the Models page in Amazon SageMaker Studio to launch a customization job, use the SageMaker Python SDK or use our Agent skills with your choice of coding assistant. To learn more, and see the list of models and supported sequence lengths per technique, see the SageMaker AI documentation .

title: AWS Secrets Manager adds managed external secrets support for Databricks and Twilio
body: AWS Secrets Manager now extends its managed external secrets capability to include Databricks and Twilio, enabling you to automatically rotate the credentials that your data pipelines and messaging applications use to call these services. You set up rotation directly from the AWS Management Console or API without writing or maintaining any custom rotation Lambda functions. Long-lived credentials often stay unrotated because rotation is hard to set up and hard to distribute safely to the applications that use the updated credential. With managed external secrets, you can use Secrets Manager to rotate the Databricks personal access tokens that your jobs and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines use. You can also rotate the service principal OAuth client secrets that your automation workflows use. Each replacement personal access token retains the scopes of the token it replaces, so a narrowly scoped token stays narrowly scoped. For Twilio, you can use Secrets Manager to rotate the API keys and Auth Tokens that your applications use to send messages and place calls. For both services, you store the credential in Secrets Manager as a managed external secret and set a rotation schedule. Secrets Manager always returns the current credential, so your applications pick up rotated values automatically, with no code changes required. These integrations join existing managed external secrets support for BigID, Cisco Security Platform, Confluent Cloud, Datadog, GitLab, Jenkins, MongoDB Atlas, Netskope, Paddle, Salesforce, Snowflake, and SonarQube. Databricks and Twilio managed external secrets are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets documentation .

title: AWS Security Hub now supports resource criticality for prioritization
body: Today, AWS Security Hub adds resource criticality to exposure prioritization, helping central security teams focus on the exposures that threaten their most business-critical resources. You can set criticality with an automation rule, for example marking every compute resource in a specific account as Very High. The rule applies to resources already in your inventory and to new resources as Security Hub discovers them. Security Hub also infers criticality from resource tags and resource names, with no configuration required, and records which source determined the value. Criticality appears as a column on the Resources page for sorting, filtering, and grouping, and on the Impact assessment tab of an exposure finding. Resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost and is always on for all customers. Resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost and requires no new enablement. To learn more, see AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page . For a list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available, see the AWS Region table .

title: Apache Iceberg materialized views now support system-managed write protection
body: Today, AWS announces system-managed materialized views for Apache Iceberg. Materialized views let you precompute an expensive query once and reuse the result across engines. Because this result is an open Iceberg table in your data lake, anyone with write access can change it, either through the catalog or by writing to the files in Amazon S3. System-managed materialized views close this gap by only allowing AWS Glue to write the materialized view's data and definition, so the result stays exactly as computed regardless of who has write access to the table or the underlying S3 files . To get started, write the SQL that defines the materialized view and, optionally, a refresh schedule. AWS Glue then computes the results, stores them as a standard Apache Iceberg table in your Amazon S3 Tables bucket, and keeps them current on your schedule. Because the result is an ordinary Iceberg table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, any Iceberg-compatible engine can read it directly, while the service guarantees no other writer can alter it. You get a governed, always-consistent dataset that you can confidently share. You can still refresh, reschedule, or drop the view whenever you need to. System-managed Apache Iceberg materialized views are available in all regions where Apache Iceberg materialized views are supported. To learn more, see System-managed materialized views in the AWS Glue Developer Guide .

title: AWS Transfer Family now supports AWS Secrets Manager storage for SFTP server host keys
body: AWS Transfer Family now lets you store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in your own AWS account. This gives you greater control over your server identity and helps simplify server migrations and failover. Previously, Transfer Family stored host keys within the service, so you could not retrieve the associated private key material. With this launch, you can choose Secrets Manager as the storage type when creating a server or importing a host key. You can then retrieve the private key material and reuse the same host key across servers and AWS Regions. For example, you can use it on a standby server for failover or on a replacement server during migration, without requiring clients to trust a new host key. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies let you control who can retrieve the stored keys. You can also migrate existing host keys to Secrets Manager, which may require additional steps; see the AWS Transfer Family User Guide for details. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transfer Family is available. To learn more, see Store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in the AWS Transfer Family User Guide. To get started, go to the AWS Transfer Family console .

title: TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 model now available on Amazon Bedrock
body: Amazon Bedrock now supports TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5, a video-to-text model that generates structured, time-coded metadata from video. Until now, finding a moment in a large video library meant knowing where to look before you could ask about it. Pegasus 1.5 reads an entire video and labels what happens and when, turning footage into data your applications can query. You define what matters to your business, such as editorial segments, speaker changes, sports plays, or brand appearances, and Pegasus 1.5 finds those moments across the video and returns them with timestamps. It analyzes what it sees, hears, and reads on screen in a single pass, with no pre-indexing or ingestion pipeline to build first. Pegasus 1.5 is accessible through the US and Global cross-Region inference profiles. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock product page, access the model in the Amazon Bedrock console, or see the Amazon Bedrock documentation for supported Regions, APIs, features, and pricing.

title: Claude Opus 4.6 now available in Amazon Bedrock
body: Starting today, Amazon Bedrock supports Claude Opus 4.6. According to Anthropic, Opus 4.6 is their most intelligent model and the world's best model for coding, enterprise agents, and professional work. Claude Opus 4.6 brings advanced capabilities to Amazon Bedrock customers, including industry-leading performance for agentic tasks, complex coding projects, and enterprise-grade workflows that require deep reasoning and reliability. Claude Opus 4.6 excels across use cases that require sophisticated reasoning and multi-step orchestration. For agentic workflows, it manages complex tasks across dozens of tools with industry-leading reliability, proactively spinning up subagents and working with less oversight. Developers can leverage Opus 4.6’s coding capabilities for long-horizon projects, complex implementations, and large-scale codebases—handling the full lifecycle from requirements gathering to implementation and maintenance. Enterprise teams can use the model to power end-to-end workflows with professional polish, including financial analysis that surfaces insights requiring days of manual compilation, cybersecurity applications that catch subtle attack patterns, and computer use workflows that move data between applications. The model supports both 200K and 1M context tokens (preview), enabling processing of extensive documents and codebases. Claude Opus 4.6 is now available in Amazon Bedrock. For the full list of available regions, refer to the documentation . To learn more and get started with the model in Amazon Bedrock, read the About Amazon blog and visit the Amazon Bedrock console .

title: Amazon Bedrock expands support for Service Quotas
body: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides secure, enterprise-grade access to high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies, enabling you to build and scale generative AI applications. Amazon Bedrock customers can now view inference quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint through AWS Service Quotas. This gives customers a familiar, consistent way to track limits for this endpoint, the same way they already do for the bedrock-runtime endpoint and other AWS services, and gives them clear visibility into the limits that apply to their workloads. The bedrock-mantle endpoint supports the OpenAI Responses API, OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Anthropic Messages API, letting customers run existing OpenAI or Anthropic based applications on Amazon Bedrock with minimal code changes. AWS Service Quotas now exposes per-model input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas for supported models on the endpoint. With this launch, customers gain visibility into how much limits they have on the bedrock-mantle endpoint and can proactively plan for production scale. To get started, open the AWS Service Quotas console, choose Amazon Bedrock, and search for "Bedrock Mantle" to view your current quotas. To request an increase to any of these quotas, follow the standard Amazon Bedrock limit increase process. Service Quotas support for the bedrock-mantle endpoint is available in all AWS Regions where the endpoint is offered: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Tokyo, Sydney, Jakarta), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Stockholm), and South America (São Paulo). To learn more, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock .

title: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights adds 25 new query commands and functions
body: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights query language now supports 25 new commands and functions that expand your ability to query, transform, correlate, and analyze logs. Customers analyzing logs in CloudWatch Logs Insights often need to perform statistical aggregation, handle null values in time-series data, compare logs across time windows, detect outliers, and enrich events with lookup data. With this launch, CloudWatch Logs Insights adds type conversion and encoding functions (hexToAscii, hexToDec, decToHex), date and time functions (parseDate, formatDate, queryStartTime, queryEndTime, queryTimeRange), string functions (messageSize), JSON inspection functions (jsonArraySize, jsonArrayContains), and a conditional validation function (isNumeric). It also introduces statistical commands (variance, topk, countFrequent), row-sequencing and null-handling commands (autoregress, accum, filldown, fillmissing), sessionization and time-comparison commands (sessionize, logcompare), a data analysis command (outlier), query-composition and join commands (where, appendcols), and a lookup enrichment command (cidrlookup). These commands and functions are available today in all commercial AWS Regions. To learn more, see the Amazon CloudWatch Logs documentation .

title: AWS Transform for full-stack Windows modernization now supports offline schema transformation to Aurora PostgreSQL
body: Today, AWS Transform for full-stack Windows modernization announced general availability of offline source transformation, enabling customers to modernize Microsoft SQL Server databases to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL without requiring a live database connection. AWS Transform now converts SQL Server storage objects, powered by AWS DMS, and code objects (stored procedures) using an agentic, interactive experience. Enterprises modernizing legacy .NET applications and their dependent SQL Server databases can now start their modernization by directly uploading the Data Design Language (DDL) source files from their databases. With offline source transformation, customers upload SQL Server data design language (DDL) files, assess database and stored procedure complexity, and generate a customizable transformation plan. AWS Transform converts tables, schemas and converts code objects such as stored procedures and functions, validates functional equivalence, and deploys the converted schema to Aurora PostgreSQL. The same workflow transforms database dependent .NET applications to be PostgreSQL compatible .NET applications with updated connection strings, ADO.NET and Entity Framework data-access calls. To address remaining conversion issues, customers can iterate directly in the web console or hand off to their preferred IDE using the AWS Transform MCP server. A separate synthetic data workflow populates Aurora PostgreSQL with test data for end-to-end application validation. AWS Transform for full-stack Windows modernization and offline source transformation is available in US East (N. Virginia). To get started, you can go to AWS Transform product page or see AWS Transform for full-stack Windows documentation .

title: AWS Partner Central agents MCP Server now supports OAuth with AWS Sign-In
body: AWS partners can now access AWS Partner Central agents from tools they already use, such as Amazon Quick and Kiro, using OAuth through AWS Sign-In. Partners can authorize agent access with their existing AWS identities, sign-in methods, IAM permissions, and governance controls without installing or maintaining additional authentication software. Previously, AWS Partners needed to set up an MCP proxy with SigV4 credentials to access Partner Central agents from their existing tools, or sign in to AWS Partner Central through the AWS Management Console with IAM credentials. OAuth simplifies this by allowing partners to use AWS Sign-In to authorize tools such as Amazon Quick and Kiro to access Partner Central agents. Partners can use OAuth from their existing tools for co-sell engagements, AWS funding applications, and AWS Marketplace seller setup. Administrators can govern access with IAM policies, global condition keys, token introspection and revocation APIs, dynamic client registration, and CloudTrail audit events. OAuth support is available to AWS Partners through AWS Partner Central agents MCP Server, which is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. To learn more, visit Getting started with the Partner Central agents MCP Server .
